stem: Maria pays $1,000 for a bond issued by a large company. In plain terms, what has she done?
options: Bought a small ownership share of the company
Lent the company money in exchange for regular interest and repayment of the $1,000 at a set date
Deposited money in an account insured by the federal government
Agreed to share in the company's profits and losses each year
explanation: A bond is an IOU: the investor is the lender, the issuer is the borrower, interest is the rent on the money and the principal is repaid at maturity (04-debt.md §2 item 1, §3.1.1). Ownership and profit-sharing describe stock; deposit insurance describes a bank account.

stem: Two years ago Dan bought a bond that pays 4% interest a year. Similar new bonds now pay 6%. If Dan tries to sell his bond today, what happens to its price?
options: It stays the same, because the issuer still pays exactly 4%
It rises, because older bonds are scarce
It rises, because the 4% payment is guaranteed
It falls, because a buyer can get 6% elsewhere and will only take Dan's bond at a discount
explanation: A bond is a fixed stream of payments; when the going rate rises, that fixed stream is worth less, so the price must fall until its yield matches the market (04-debt.md §2 items 3-4, §3.4.5).

stem: A rating agency gives a company's bonds a very low rating. What does this MOST directly tell an investor?
options: There is a higher chance the company will fail to make its interest or principal payments
The bond's price will fall sharply if interest rates rise
The company pays interest less often than other issuers
The bond cannot be sold before it matures
explanation: Ratings measure default (credit) risk only, not interest-rate risk, payment frequency or liquidity (04-debt.md §3.8.1). A low rating is like a bad credit score for the borrower.

stem: A company goes out of business and its assets are sold to pay everyone it owes. Which group is generally paid FIRST?
options: Common stockholders
Preferred stockholders
Lenders whose bonds are backed by specific company property
No one is first; all claims are paid in equal proportion
explanation: Secured creditors are paid first from their collateral, then unsecured creditors, then preferred and finally common stockholders (04-debt.md §3.2.3 liquidation priority). Stockholders are owners, not lenders, and stand last in line.

stem: A retiree splits her savings evenly among bonds that come due one, two, three, four and five years from now. Each time one matures she buys a new five-year bond. What is the MAIN benefit of this approach?
options: It guarantees the highest possible return
Some money comes due every year, so she is never locked into a single interest rate and always has cash coming available
It removes the risk that any issuer fails to pay
It avoids income tax on the interest
explanation: This is a bond ladder: staggered maturities average out reinvestment risk and provide regular liquidity at a moderate yield, the default conservative-retiree strategy (04-debt.md §3.15). It does not maximize return, eliminate default risk or change taxation.

stem: A corporate bond that is backed only by the issuer's general promise to pay, with no specific assets pledged as collateral, is a:
options: Mortgage bond
Equipment trust certificate
Debenture
Collateral trust bond
explanation: Debentures are unsecured and backed by the issuer's full faith and credit; mortgage bonds, equipment trust certificates and collateral trust bonds are all secured by specific pledged assets (04-debt.md §3.2.1-3.2.2).

stem: Which of the following agency securities is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government?
options: Ginnie Mae (GNMA) pass-through certificates
Fannie Mae (FNMA) mortgage-backed securities
Freddie Mac (FHLMC) mortgage-backed securities
Federal Home Loan Bank debentures
explanation: GNMA is a government corporation within HUD and its pass-throughs are the only MBS carrying the full faith and credit of the U.S. government; FNMA and FHLMC are GSEs with implicit backing and FHLB is a GSE lender (04-debt.md §3.10.1-3.10.3).

stem: Interest received on a U.S. Treasury note is:
options: Exempt from federal income tax but subject to state income tax
Subject to federal, state and local income tax
Exempt from federal, state and local income tax
Subject to federal income tax but exempt from state and local income tax
explanation: Treasury interest is federally taxable and exempt from state and local tax; the reverse-attribute distractor (federal-exempt, state-taxable) describes nothing, and fully taxable describes GNMA/FNMA/FHLMC and corporates (04-debt.md §3.9, §3.17).

stem: Commercial paper is BEST described as:
options: A bank-guaranteed time draft used to finance imports and exports
An unsecured short-term promissory note issued by a corporation, with a maximum maturity of 270 days
A short-term note secured by the issuer's real property
A bank time deposit that pays interest at maturity
explanation: Commercial paper is unsecured corporate paper sold at a discount with maturities of 270 days or less, which keeps it exempt from 1933 Act registration (04-debt.md §3.12). The time draft is a banker's acceptance and the interest-paying deposit is a negotiable CD.

stem: When short-term Treasury yields are higher than long-term Treasury yields, the yield curve is described as:
options: Normal
Flat
Inverted
Humped
explanation: An inverted (negative) curve has short rates above long rates, typically during Fed tightening when markets expect cuts; a normal curve slopes upward, a flat curve shows little difference and a humped curve peaks at intermediate maturities (04-debt.md §3.14).

stem: A corporate bond is quoted at 98 3/8. What is the dollar price of one bond?
explanation: Corporate bonds are quoted as a percentage of $1,000 par in eighths: 3/8 = 0.375, so 98.375% x $1,000 = $983.75 (04-debt.md §3.4.1). $980.94 applies Treasury 32nds; $98.38 forgets to multiply by $1,000.

stem: A Treasury bond is quoted at 101-12. What is the dollar price of one bond?
explanation: Treasury notes and bonds are quoted in 32nds: 101-12 = 101 + 12/32 = 101.375% of $1,000 = $1,013.75 (04-debt.md §3.4.2). $1,011.20 reads the quote as the decimal 101.12%; $1,015.00 would be 101-16 (a half point), not 101-12; $1,012.00 treats the 12 as $12.

stem: A 6% corporate bond is trading at 90. What is its current yield?
explanation: Current yield = annual interest / market price = $60 / $900 = 6.67% (04-debt.md §3.5.2). 6.00% is the nominal yield and 7.37% is the approximate 10-year YTM, both distractors.

stem: Which of the following is the LOWEST rating that is still considered investment grade by Standard & Poor's?
options: A-
BB+
BBB
BBB-
explanation: Investment grade covers the top four categories, down to and including BBB- (S&P/Fitch) or Baa3 (Moody's); BB+ and below is high-yield (04-debt.md §3.8.1).

stem: A bond has a duration of 7. If market interest rates rise by 1%, the bond's price will most likely:
options: Fall by approximately 7%
Rise by approximately 7%
Fall by approximately 1%
Fall by approximately 14%
explanation: Percentage price change is approximately -duration x change in yield: -7 x 1% = -7% (a $1,000 bond to about $930) (04-debt.md §3.7.2). Direction is inverse; magnitude is the duration, not 1% or double.

stem: An 8% corporate bond pays interest on January 15 and July 15. A customer buys one bond ($1,000 par) on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, with regular-way settlement. How much accrued interest does the buyer pay the seller?
explanation: Regular way is T+1, so settlement is Wednesday March 11, 2026. Using 30/360, count January 15 up to but not including March 11: 16 (Jan) + 30 (Feb) + 10 (Mar) = 56 days; $80 x 56/360 = $12.44 (04-debt.md §3.6.4). $12.67 counts 57 days by including the settlement date; $12.22 uses 55 days.

stem: A 5% convertible bond with a conversion price of $25 is trading at $1,080. The issuer's common stock is trading at $28. What arbitrage profit per bond, before commissions, is available?
options: None, because the bond is trading above parity
explanation: Conversion ratio = $1,000 / $25 = 40 shares; parity price of the bond = $28 x 40 = $1,120. The bond at $1,080 is below parity, so buy the bond, convert and sell 40 shares at $28 for $1,120, a $40 profit (04-debt.md §3.3.1-3.3.2). The coupon is a distractor.

stem: A 6% bond with 10 years to maturity is purchased at $1,100. It is callable in 5 years at 103. Using the exam approximation method, the yield to call is closest to:
explanation: YTC = [annual interest + (call price - purchase price) / years to call] / [(call price + purchase price) / 2] = [$60 + ($1,030 - $1,100)/5] / [($1,030 + $1,100)/2] = $46 / $1,065 = 4.32% (04-debt.md §3.5.4). 4.76% is the approximate YTM and 5.45% the current yield; on a premium bond YTC is the lowest.

stem: An investor buys a $1,000 Treasury Inflation-Protected Security with a 3% coupon. Over the first year the CPI rises 4%. Approximately how much interest will the investor receive for that year?
explanation: TIPS keep the coupon rate fixed and adjust the principal for CPI: $1,000 x 1.04 = $1,040 adjusted principal, and 3% of $1,040 = $31.20 (04-debt.md §3.9.4). The inflation adjustment raises principal (taxed annually as phantom income), not the coupon rate.

stem: A 182-day Treasury bill is purchased at $97.50 per $100 of face value. What is its annualized discount yield?
explanation: Discount yield = (par - price) / par x 360 / days = (100 - 97.50) / 100 x 360 / 182 = 4.95% (04-debt.md §3.4.3). 5.14% is the bond-equivalent yield (divides by price and uses 365 days); 2.50% is the unannualized discount.

stem: A 5% corporate bond with 10 years to maturity is trading at 102. It is callable in 5 years at 103. Using the exam approximation formulas, which of the bond's yields is the LOWEST?
options: Nominal yield
Current yield
Yield to maturity
Yield to call
explanation: Current yield = $50 / $1,020 = 4.90%. YTM = [$50 + ($1,000 - $1,020)/10] / [($1,000 + $1,020)/2] = $48 / $1,010 = 4.75%. YTC = [$50 + ($1,030 - $1,020)/5] / [($1,030 + $1,020)/2] = $52 / $1,025 = 5.07%. The memorized rule 'premium bond: nominal > CY > YTM > YTC' assumes a call at or near par. Here the call price (103) is ABOVE the market price (102), so a call hands the holder a gain instead of a loss and YTC becomes the HIGHEST yield. Ordering: YTC 5.07% > nominal 5.00% > CY 4.90% > YTM 4.75%, so YTM is lowest (04-debt.md §3.5.3-3.5.6).

stem: Which of the following CMO tranches would be expected to INCREASE in value when market interest rates rise?
options: Principal-only (PO) tranche
Planned amortization class (PAC) tranche
Interest-only (IO) tranche
Z (accrual) tranche
explanation: Rising rates slow prepayments, so the mortgage interest stream lasts longer and the IO tranche gains value; it is the one bond-like security whose price moves with rates (04-debt.md §3.11.2). POs benefit from faster prepayments, and PAC and Z tranches lose value like ordinary bonds.

stem: All of the following statements about Ginnie Mae (GNMA) pass-through certificates are true EXCEPT:
options: They are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government
Investors receive monthly payments of both interest and principal
The underlying pools consist of FHA, VA or USDA-insured mortgages
Interest received is exempt from state and local income taxes
explanation: GNMA interest is fully taxable at the federal, state and local levels; only Treasuries and the FHLB/FFCB/TVA lenders get the state exemption (04-debt.md §3.10.1, §3.17). The other three statements are the classic true attributes of GNMA pass-throughs.

stem: A dealer quotes a Treasury bill as bid 4.30, ask 4.25. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The bid represents a lower dollar price than the ask, because T-bills are quoted on a discount-yield basis
The bid represents a higher dollar price than the ask, as with any other security
A customer buying the bill from the dealer will pay a price based on the 4.30 yield
The quote is expressed as a percentage of par in 32nds
explanation: T-bills are quoted as annualized discount yields, so the higher number is the lower dollar price; the dealer bids to buy at the higher yield (lower price) and offers at the lower yield (04-debt.md §3.4.3). A customer buys at the ask, 4.25, and 32nds apply to notes and bonds, not bills.

stem: A 4% Treasury note pays interest on February 15 and August 15. A customer buys the note on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, for regular-way settlement. How many days of accrued interest will the buyer pay?
explanation: Treasuries settle T+1 (Wednesday March 11) and accrue on actual calendar days from the last coupon up to but not including settlement: February 15-28 = 14 days, plus March 1-10 = 10 days, for 24 days (04-debt.md §3.6.5). 26 applies the corporate 30/360 count to a Treasury; 25 and 27 wrongly include the settlement date.
